title: Urinary Incontinence in Older Adults: Classify the Pattern Before Prescribing
bottomLine: Urinary incontinence is a syndrome, not an inevitable part of aging. Separate urgency, stress, overflow/retention, functional and mixed patterns; look for reversible contributors and mobility/cognition barriers before adding bladder medication.
recognize: Urgency/frequency suggests overactive-bladder physiology; leakage with cough/exertion suggests stress incontinence; weak stream/high residual suggests retention/overflow.
Delirium, constipation, infection symptoms, diuretics, sedatives, mobility barriers and inaccessible toileting can worsen continence.
differentiate: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not a diagnosis of symptomatic UTI and should not explain chronic incontinence by itself.
Functional incontinence may improve more from mobility/environment changes than from bladder drugs.
assessment: Review onset, urgency/stress symptoms, voiding pattern, nocturia, dysuria/hematuria, retention symptoms, bowel function, mobility/cognition, fluids, medications, pelvic/prostate history and goals.
workup: Use urinalysis when infection/hematuria is clinically plausible and post-void residual when retention/overflow is suspected; avoid indiscriminate urine cultures in asymptomatic patients.
management: Use bladder training, timed/prompted voiding, pelvic-floor therapy, constipation/mobility/environment changes and cause-specific treatment.
Medication is individualized after anticholinergic/cognitive/falls burden and retention risk are considered.
medicationSafety: Antimuscarinics can worsen dry mouth, constipation, retention and cognitive burden; review total anticholinergic exposure.
Do not treat a positive urine culture without compatible urinary/systemic infection.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and normalize assessment while avoiding the message that leakage is simply expected with age.
followUp: Track symptom pattern, function, adverse effects and residual when indicated; refer persistent retention, hematuria or refractory disease.
examTrap: Starting an anticholinergic for every older adult with leakage without checking retention, cognition, constipation, mobility and medications.
oneLinePearl: Classify the leakage first; sometimes the best bladder treatment is mobility, bowel or medication care.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada geriatrics/family-medicine urinary stewardship

title: Constipation in Older Adults: Medication, Mobility, Hydration, Outlet, or Obstruction?
bottomLine: Constipation is common but not automatically benign. Define stool frequency/consistency and evacuation difficulty, review medications, intake, mobility and pelvic-floor factors, and look for impaction, obstruction, bleeding or weight-loss red flags before escalating laxatives.
recognize: Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, dehydration, immobility and neurologic disease are common contributors.
Fecal impaction can paradoxically present with overflow diarrhea or delirium/urinary symptoms.
differentiate: Chronic functional constipation differs from acute obstruction or new bowel-habit change with alarm features.
Docusate alone is low-value for opioid-induced constipation compared with effective stimulant/osmotic bowel regimens.
assessment: Review duration, stool form, straining/incomplete evacuation, pain/distension, bleeding, weight change, medications, fluids/fibre, mobility, cognition and rectal symptoms; perform abdominal/rectal exam when indicated.
workup: Routine broad labs/imaging are unnecessary for uncomplicated chronic constipation; use targeted CBC/chemistry/TSH/calcium, colon evaluation or imaging when alarm features or secondary causes are plausible.
management: Address medication and mobility factors, use adequate fluids/fibre when appropriate and evidence-based osmotic/stimulant therapy matched to cause.
Opioid therapy should include an effective prophylactic bowel plan unless contraindicated.
medicationSafety: Avoid magnesium/phosphate products without considering renal function and electrolyte risk.
Do not repeatedly intensify laxatives in suspected obstruction/impaction without assessment.
counselling: Set realistic bowel goals and explain that daily stool is not required if passage is comfortable and regular for the patient.
followUp: Reassess response, adherence and secondary contributors; investigate refractory/new-onset disease appropriately.
examTrap: Adding docusate alone to chronic opioid therapy and assuming constipation prevention is complete.
oneLinePearl: Treat constipation by mechanism—and never let a bowel regimen hide obstruction or impaction.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada palliative-care constipation recommendations

title: Unintentional Weight Loss in Older Adults: Appetite Is Not the Diagnosis
bottomLine: Unintentional weight loss is a geriatric red flag. Confirm the trajectory and assess intake/access, swallowing/dentition, medications, depression/cognition, GI/endocrine disease, malignancy, inflammation and social isolation rather than prescribing supplements before finding the cause.
recognize: Weight loss, reduced muscle mass/strength, loose clothing, declining ADLs and reduced intake can precede obvious disease.
Food insecurity, grief, caregiver stress, dysphagia and medication adverse effects are common and treatable contributors.
differentiate: Frailty/cachexia, malnutrition and sarcopenia overlap but are not identical.
Intentional weight reduction should still be reconsidered when frailty, falls or muscle loss emerges.
assessment: Verify serial weight/BMI and recent trajectory; assess diet, appetite, swallowing, dentition, GI symptoms, mood/cognition, medications, alcohol, finances/food access, malignancy/infection symptoms and function.
workup: Use targeted CBC/chemistry/TSH and disease-specific testing based on symptoms/exam; avoid indiscriminate tumor-marker panels or imaging without a clinical differential.
management: Treat reversible cause, improve meal support/access/oral health/swallowing, use dietitian and resistance/activity strategies, and align goals with frailty/illness context.
Oral supplements can support intake but do not replace diagnostic workup or meals/social supports.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine appetite stimulants when harms outweigh modest benefit; review drugs causing nausea, dry mouth, sedation or anorexia.
redFlags: Refeeding risk after prolonged poor intake
counselling: Discuss nutrition without weight stigma and include food access, cultural preference and caregiver capacity.
followUp: Trend weight, strength/function and intake; close diagnostic and social-service referrals.
examTrap: Prescribing a nutrition shake and calling the problem solved without evaluating dysphagia, depression, medications, malignancy or food insecurity.
oneLinePearl: Older-adult weight loss is a symptom with medical and social causes—find the driver.

title: Sleep Problems in Older Adults: Diagnose the Sleep Disorder Before Sedating It
bottomLine: Insomnia, sleep apnea, restless legs, circadian disruption, nocturia, pain and mood disorders require different treatment. Start with sleep history and reversible contributors; non-drug insomnia treatment is preferred before sedative-hypnotics because older adults have disproportionate falls, cognitive and driving harm.
recognize: Insomnia causes difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep with daytime impact despite opportunity; OSA causes snoring/apneas/sleep fragmentation and sleepiness; restless legs has an urge-to-move pattern.
differentiate: Reduced total sleep with normal daytime function can reflect age-related change rather than insomnia disorder.
Daytime sleepiness is not automatically insomnia and should prompt OSA/medication/neurologic review.
assessment: Review schedule/naps, caffeine/alcohol, snoring/apneas, leg symptoms, pain, nocturia, mood, cognition, medications, falls and daytime driving risk.
workup: Sleep study is targeted to suspected sleep-disordered breathing/other specific sleep disease, not routine for primary insomnia.
management: Use CBT-I/stimulus control/sleep consolidation for chronic insomnia and treat OSA/restless legs/pain/nocturia/mood contributors.
If medication is used, choose the narrowest indication/lowest effective exposure with a stop/reassessment plan.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines/Z-drugs and sedating anticholinergic OTC products increase falls/confusion; avoid routine first-line use.
Review combined opioids/alcohol/other sedatives for respiratory and cognitive risk.
counselling: Explain that non-drug sleep treatment can outperform chronic sedative escalation and avoids next-day impairment.
followUp: Track sleep efficiency, daytime function and falls; deprescribe chronic sedatives gradually when appropriate.
examTrap: Starting a benzodiazepine for an older adult's insomnia before asking about OSA, falls, alcohol, nocturia and medications.
oneLinePearl: Treat the sleep disorder—not wakefulness with a sedative.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Geriatrics and Hospital Pharmacy recommendations

title: Chronic Pain in Older Adults: Function, Mechanism, and Multimodal Safety
bottomLine: Chronic pain management should improve function and quality of life while minimizing falls, delirium, constipation, renal/GI toxicity and dependence. Define the pain mechanism and patient goals, optimize non-drug and non-opioid therapy first, and use opioids only when benefits clearly exceed harms with monitoring and a stopping plan.
recognize: Nociceptive, neuropathic and centralized pain respond differently; cognition/sensory impairment may alter how pain is communicated.
Pain can worsen mobility, mood, sleep and frailty, while treatment itself can worsen those same outcomes.
differentiate: New severe pain, night/systemic symptoms or focal neurologic deficit requires diagnostic evaluation rather than chronic-pain escalation.
Palliative/end-of-life opioid decisions differ from routine chronic non-cancer pain.
assessment: Assess location/mechanism, function, mood/sleep, falls, cognition, renal/hepatic/GI risk, medications/substances, prior therapies and patient-defined goals.
workup: Use imaging/labs only when red flags or a specific treatable diagnosis makes them useful; routine repeat imaging for stable chronic pain is low value.
management: Prioritize exercise/rehabilitation, psychological/self-management strategies and mechanism-appropriate non-opioid therapy.
If an opioid trial is justified, define functional benefit, lowest effective exposure, safety monitoring and discontinuation criteria.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs require renal/GI/CV risk review; gabapentinoids/TCAs/SNRIs require falls/cognition/interaction review; opioids add sedation, constipation, falls and overdose risk.
redFlags: Pain with acute ischemic/visceral emergency features
counselling: Set goals around activity/sleep/self-care rather than promising zero pain and discuss medication risks transparently.
followUp: Reassess function, harms and continued indication; taper ineffective/high-risk medication rather than escalating indefinitely.
examTrap: Escalating chronic opioids because pain score remains high despite no functional improvement and increasing falls/sedation.
oneLinePearl: In geriatric pain, function and treatment harm are outcomes equal to the pain score.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Family Medicine/Hospital Pharmacy chronic-pain recommendations

title: Osteoporosis in Older Adults: Fracture Risk, Falls, Treatment, and Safe Transitions
bottomLine: Osteoporosis care prevents fractures, not merely low BMD. Assess prior fragility fracture and current fracture risk, falls, secondary causes, renal/dental/medication factors and goals; use evidence-based antiresorptive/anabolic therapy where benefit is meaningful and never stop denosumab without a transition plan.
recognize: Prior hip/vertebral/recent fragility fracture and falls strongly raise near-term risk.
A vertebral fracture may be clinically silent and present as height loss/kyphosis.
differentiate: Osteoporosis treatment is risk-based; one T-score is not the entire decision.
Frailty/limited life expectancy changes time-to-benefit discussions but does not erase fracture prevention automatically.
assessment: Review fractures/falls, height loss, glucocorticoids, smoking/alcohol, calcium/vitamin D intake, renal disease, dental issues, mobility and secondary causes.
workup: Use Canadian FRAX with BMD when appropriate and targeted labs for secondary disease/drug suitability; image for suspected vertebral fracture when indicated.
management: Use resistance/balance exercise, nutrition and falls prevention plus pharmacotherapy according to Osteoporosis Canada risk thresholds and patient goals.
Bisphosphonates are first-line for many; denosumab requires uninterrupted therapy or planned antiresorptive transition.
medicationSafety: Review renal suitability and administration for bisphosphonates; assess hypocalcemia risk with denosumab and jaw/atypical-femur symptoms when relevant.
Do not create a denosumab 'drug holiday'.
redFlags: Acute severe back pain with neurologic compromise
counselling: Explain absolute fracture risk and time-to-benefit rather than focusing only on a BMD number.
followUp: Monitor adherence/new fractures and repeat BMD/risk at guideline-appropriate intervals or earlier with new risk.
examTrap: Stopping denosumab without follow-on antiresorptive therapy because the BMD improved.
oneLinePearl: Osteoporosis treatment follows fracture risk—and denosumab needs an exit strategy.

title: Vision and Hearing Loss: Sensory Function Changes Falls, Cognition, and Communication
bottomLine: Sensory loss is not a harmless inconvenience: it worsens falls, isolation, medication errors, delirium and apparent cognitive impairment. Confirm the sensory deficit, identify reversible/urgent causes and optimize communication devices/environment before labelling an older adult confused or nonadherent.
recognize: Presbycusis commonly causes high-frequency hearing loss; cataract/refractive disease are common visual causes, but sudden loss has a different urgency.
differentiate: Cerumen/medication/acute ear disease can mimic chronic hearing loss.
Sudden monocular vision loss, acute angle-closure symptoms, retinal detachment symptoms and sudden sensorineural hearing loss are emergencies/urgent specialty conditions.
assessment: Ask functional hearing/vision difficulty, falls, driving, communication, tinnitus/vertigo, eye pain/flashes/floaters and device use; inspect ears and assess visual acuity when possible.
workup: Use audiology/ophthalmology/optometry assessment for persistent deficits and urgent specialty evaluation for sudden/acute red flags.
management: Treat reversible causes, optimize hearing aids/visual correction, lighting/communication strategies and falls safety.
medicationSafety: Review ototoxic drugs and medications contributing to dizziness/blurred vision; avoid attributing sensory impairment to dementia before correcting modifiable deficits.
counselling: Use face-to-face clear communication and verify understanding rather than assuming hearing/cognition failure.
followUp: Close sensory referrals and reassess falls/communication after correction.
examTrap: Calling an older adult cognitively impaired when they cannot hear the assessment questions or see the instructions.
oneLinePearl: Correct the senses before judging cognition, adherence or function.

title: Driving Safety: Function, Cognition, Vision, Medications, and Jurisdictional Duty
bottomLine: Driving fitness is a functional safety assessment, not an age cutoff. Evaluate cognition/executive function, vision, motor ability, reaction time, syncope/seizure risk, sleepiness, medications/substances and crash/near-miss history, then follow provincial or territorial reporting rules and referral pathways.
recognize: Family concern, getting lost, new crashes, traffic violations, delayed reactions and medication/syncope events can signal risk.
One brief cognitive score cannot independently prove safe or unsafe driving.
differentiate: A diagnosis such as dementia does not map perfectly to driving ability at every stage; actual function and jurisdictional standards matter.
Temporary restrictions after syncope/seizure/acute illness differ from progressive cognitive driving risk.
assessment: Ask patient/family about incidents, navigation, compensatory behaviours, vision/hearing, mobility, cognition, sleepiness, alcohol/cannabis, medications and relevant neurologic/cardiac events.
workup: Use focused cognitive/visual/physical testing and formal on-road/occupational driving assessment when clinical uncertainty remains and local pathways support it.
management: Treat reversible contributors, reduce impairing medications, discuss restriction/cessation when risk is unacceptable and follow jurisdictional reporting obligations.
Plan alternative transportation to reduce isolation and preserve access to care.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics and other impairing drugs should be reviewed before declaring risk unavoidable.
counselling: Frame driving as safety/function, not punishment, and involve supports while respecting confidentiality/legal duties.
followUp: Document reasoning, reporting/referral actions and reassess if function or treatment changes.
examTrap: Using age or one cognitive test score as the sole reason to remove or retain driving privileges.
oneLinePearl: Driving is a functional task; assess the abilities and risks that the task requires.

title: Elder Abuse: Safety, Capacity, Dependence, and the Older Adult's Voice
bottomLine: Elder abuse can be physical, psychological, sexual, financial or neglect and often occurs within dependency relationships. Assess privately when possible, determine immediate danger and decision-specific capacity, document objectively and use provincial/territorial adult-protection, substitute-decision or emergency pathways rather than assuming every capable adult must accept the clinician's preferred solution.
recognize: Unexplained injuries, fearfulness, medication/food deprivation, coercive control, unusual financial changes, caregiver behaviour or recurrent missed care can be clues.
Cognitive impairment, isolation, dependence and caregiver stress increase vulnerability but do not prove abuse.
differentiate: A capable adult may choose a risky relationship; incapacity, coercion or immediate danger changes the intervention options.
Self-neglect can reflect capacity, depression, dementia, poverty or access barriers and requires assessment rather than moral judgment.
assessment: Interview privately when safe; ask directly about harm/control/finances/neglect, assess injuries, medication/food access, cognition/capacity, caregiver dependence, social network and immediate safety.
workup: Use injury/sexual-assault/financial/capacity evaluation as indicated; preserve/document evidence objectively without turning the clinical interview into a forensic interrogation.
management: Treat urgent harm, create a safety plan and involve social work/adult-protection/police/emergency services according to capacity, consent, severity and jurisdictional law.
Do not confront a suspected abuser in a way that increases risk before a safe plan is established.
medicationSafety: Review medication withholding/overmedication and controlled-drug access when abuse or exploitation is suspected.
counselling: Validate concerns, preserve the older adult's autonomy where capacity permits and explain reporting/confidentiality limits honestly.
followUp: Close safety/social/legal referrals and reassess when the older adult remains in a high-risk environment.
examTrap: Assuming cognitive impairment automatically removes the older adult's autonomy—or insisting a capable adult follow a safety plan without assessing their wishes and legal context.
oneLinePearl: Protect safety without erasing autonomy; capacity and jurisdiction determine the path.
